title: I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:6–8)
hookLine: Paul near the end: I have fought a good fight, kept the faith
tomorrow: does God still speak today, or has he said it all?

cards: Final messages are supposed to sound final. In the movie version there's a speech, a hand squeezed, a long look out a window.
Near the end of Second Timothy, the writer is a prisoner who says his time is close, and he does write the big lines.
Then, a few verses later, this: "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments." A coat. Something to read.

teach.b: First, the big lines. "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand."
Then three short ones: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Three verbs, all done. The King James says course; the title says race.
A runner's picture: the track laid out, run to the end. He doesn't say he won, or was fastest. He says he finished, and kept what was handed to him, the way someone keeps a promise.

Then: "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness," and right away, "not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing." The finish line isn't a podium for one. Now the puzzle.
Why the coat? Because finishing a course isn't the same as being finished with living.
The man who has kept the faith is still cold, still wants to read, still misses his friends. Come soon, he writes; only Luke is with me.
Faith kept to the end still asks for a coat, and the letter isn't embarrassed about it. One more line to tell a friend tonight.
At his first hearing, he says, everyone deserted him, and then: "I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge." Finishing well, here, includes letting the ones who ran off the hook.

how: Some Christians read 2 Timothy 4:6–8 at funerals or near the end of a long service, as words for a life finished faithfully.

games.q: what does “i have finished the race” mean?
o: a course run to the end, the faith kept
giving up because the end is too close
first place won after a long contest

games.q: three verbs and a coat — tap the pairs.

s: 'I have finished my course' means Paul won the race
he says fought, finished, kept the faith: no word about winning.
in the same chapter, Paul asks for his coat and his books
"the cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus… and the books, but especially the parchments."
Paul says the crown is for him alone
"not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing."

games.q: your coach retires and says at the banquet, 'i didn't win the most, but i finished.' someone whispers that's a sad thing to say. how does 2 Timothy 4 hear it?
o: as Paul's own kind of words: not won, but finished, and faith kept.
as giving up, since finishing only counts if you won.
as false modesty that Paul would have corrected.
games.why: Paul doesn't claim to have won or been fastest. he says fought, finished, kept, and the crown is for all who love his appearing.

practice: Choose one small thing you've left half done that you can finish right where you are: a drawer, a reply, a loose button, a cup to rinse. Do the last step slowly and fully, so that when the sit begins, that one thing is finished.
Then notice what it's like to have one thing done and put away.

wordCard.voice: I have finished the race. Paul's words near the end of Second Timothy: the course run to the end, the faith kept, and still a coat to ask for.

orig.note: Greek: course, race; the King James renders it course in 2 Timothy 4:7.

carryVoice: The line to keep: I have kept the faith, finished and kept, and then, bring the coat. Rest well.
